title: Op-Ed: EA didn’t close BioWare, it slowly killed a legendary studio
summary: MANILA, Philippines – Bioware is shutting down. Bloomberg broke the story with a report that parent company Electronic Arts would be cutting around 400 jobs, about three percent of the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Bioware is shutting down. Bloomberg broke the story with a report that parent company Electronic Arts would be cutting around 400 jobs, about three percent of the company’s staff, including the roughly 50 people who remain at the Canadian studio. A fifth Mass Effect game was in reportedly in development, but is now canceled, with Bloomberg citing an internal memo from EA CEO David Tinson and chief studios officer Cam Weber.

“Now, after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending,” BioWare wrote in a post on X that effectively confirmed Bloomberg’s report. “There is nothing easy about writing those words. Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition.”
pic.twitter.com/TicSujMWps— BioWare (@bioware) October 21, 2026
The end of a storied developer

EA for its part, had only ruthless, cold-blooded words to spare, doling out a token thanks to employees before immediately telling them some of them would be losing their jobs. “Today, we’re the number one publisher in Western HD gaming. That’s an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of,” read Tinson and Weber’s memo, which was published later in the day.

The news came as a blow, understandably due to the outsized impact of Bioware’s extensive catalog of role-playing games. These include bonafide PC classics like Baldur’s Gate and its sequel Baldur’s Gate II: Shadows of Amn, as well as Neverwinter Nights. The Edmonton-based studio also developed Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, regarded by many as one of the best Star Wars games of all time.

After several partnerships with Interplay, LucasArts and Microsoft, Bioware was acquired in 2007 by Electronic Arts. Under the publisher, they began a streak of big budget console RPGs that brought their work to a wider audience and greater acclaim. These include the original Mass Effect trilogy and the Dragon Age series. Bioware Austin was set up to develop the MMO Star Wars: The Old Republic.

Same old story with a notorious publisher

But like many studios under the EA umbrella, Bioware struggled to thrive, despite the blockbuster success of Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Bioware reportedly encountered many obstacles and challenges. Producer Mark Darrah and director David Gaider recounted difficulties getting resources approved for Dragon Age, a series largely considered by EA leadership to be the lesser of the studios’ franchises.

Although 2014’s Dragon Age: Inquisition was critically praised and exceeded internal sales projections, it also reflected a directive to chase design trends such as live service elements and engagement-driven mechanics. This continued in 2016’s Mass Effect: Andromeda and culminated in 2019’s Anthem, a loot shooter with impressive technology but an underbaked world with repetitive gameplay.

Yet despite the studio’s compliance, EA continued to yank its chain around. Corporate leadership kept pushing all of its studios to use the Frostbite engine that was developed by DICE for the Battlefield series. For Bioware that meant trying to build action role-playing games using technology developed for a multiplayer shooter, while fighting in the queue for the small team in charge of providing technical support for the engine.

The amount of support received on Frostbite was based on how much money your game was projected to make, said one dev and EA reportedly expected very little out of Dragon Age, no matter how many times it beat corporate’s expectations. And the reward for success was that Bioware’s programmers got sent to FIFA, taking any Frostbite expertise they acquired on projects like Dragon Age Inquisition with them.

The last game released by Bioware was 2024’s Dragon Age: The Veilguard, a game that released to mostly positive critical reception but divided fans on its tone and handle on the series’ lore and worldbuilding. The game sold a surprising amount, considering weak marketing for a moribund IP, but well below the expectations EA set for a project built on over a decade of false starts, including one as a live service game.
The autopsy reveals a studio’s gradual death

Bioware was not without its own problems. EA’s marketing departments always played favorites with the Mass Effect team, which led to attitude and bred resentment from the Dragon Age team. And as their games became more technologically elaborate, the writers who created beloved characters and stories were seen as unnecessary. Over the past decade, many of the writers who were foundational to the studio’s work have been laid off.

For many, Bioware’s closure is more than just a disappointment, it’s a heartbreaking reminder that the people who make games are ultimately nothing more than disposable assets and line items on a spreadsheet. And while it could be argued that the Bioware of recent years is not the same studio that it used to be, it doesn’t heal the hearts of those who were rooting for them to recover.

For as polarizing as Veilguard was, there was enough to see that enough to see that the studio still had it in them to make good single-player companion-centered role-playing games, even if the specifics could use some work. It was enough to hope that the fifth Mass Effect game that was being relentlessly teased for nearly a decade, might deliver on some of what people genuinely like about Bioware games.

The end of Bioware means an end to what was once an influential force in Western RPGs and a refuge (albeit an imperfect one) for LGBTQ gamers. There’s a sense of disbelief hanging over the cancellation of the next Mass Effect and a particular glee among bigots who support a Saudi investment fund unwilling to sign off on “woke” games. But it doesn’t matter what the last nail in the coffin was, it was EA that ensured Bioware’s slow death.
